desc:
The distance between two nodes of a tree is the number of edges on the path connecting them; the path may go up towards the root and then down again.

Given a binary tree, the value target of one of its nodes and an integer k, return the values of all nodes whose distance from the target node is exactly k. The values may be returned in any order; if there is no such node, return an empty array.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For the tree below ([3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, -1, -1, 7, 4]) with target = 5: k = 2 gives [1, 4, 7] (any order) and k = 3 gives [0, 8].

        3
      /   \
     5     1
    / \   / \
   6   2 0   8
      / \
     7   4
constraints: All node values are distinct, so a value identifies exactly one node
The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Going down from the target is easy. The hard part is nodes reached by first going up to an ancestor.
A tree is a graph in which every edge can be walked in both directions. If every node knew its parent, you could treat the tree as an undirected graph.

Record each node's parent, then run a breadth-first search from the target over the three neighbours (left, right, parent), tracking a visited set. The nodes found at BFS level exactly k are the answer.
editorial: Add the missing 'up' edges: one pass over the array gives the parent of every node. Now every node has up to three neighbours and a breadth-first search from the target visits nodes in increasing order of distance. Stop after level k and report the nodes of that level. A visited set (or remembering the node we came from) prevents going back.

Time and space are O(n). An alternative is a recursive method that returns the distance from the current node to the target and, on the way back, collects nodes at the remaining distance in the sibling subtree; it needs no parent pointers but is easier to get wrong.
